title: Public Law (Constitutional and Administrative)
topics: The UK constitution: sources and nature
Rule of law and separation of powers

notes.h: The UK constitution: sources and nature
notes.body:
The UK has no single codified constitutional document. Its constitution is found in several sources, some legal and some political, and most of it can be changed by ordinary Act of Parliament.

Sources
- Statute: Magna Carta (three chapters of the 1297 version remain in force), the Bill of Rights 1689, the Acts of Union 1706–07 and 1800, the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, the European Communities Act 1972 (repealed), the Human Rights Act 1998, the devolution Acts, the Constitutional Reform Act 2005, the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 and the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022.
- Common law: case law recognising fundamental rights and controlling the prerogative, e.g. Entick v Carrington (1765) and the Case of Proclamations (1610).
- Constitutional conventions: binding political rules that courts recognise but do not enforce, such as the requirement of royal assent to Bills passed by Parliament and ministerial responsibility.
- The law and custom of Parliament, including parliamentary privilege.
- Authoritative works such as Dicey, Bagehot and Erskine May, and soft-law texts such as the Cabinet Manual and Ministerial Code.

Characteristics
- Uncodified, and largely flexible: there is no special amendment procedure.
- Unitary but devolved, rather than federal.
- A constitutional monarchy with parliamentary government: the executive is drawn from and accountable to Parliament, so powers are fused to a degree.
- Political constitutionalism: accountability is mostly through Parliament and elections. Griffith (1979) argued the constitution is 'no more and no less than what happens'. Legal constitutionalists such as Allan stress the courts' role in protecting fundamental values.

Constitutional statutes
Laws LJ in Thoburn v Sunderland CC (2002) suggested certain statutes are 'constitutional statutes' that cannot be impliedly repealed, only expressly or by unavoidably clear words. The Supreme Court in R (HS2 Action Alliance) v Transport Secretary (2014) suggested that some constitutional principles may prevail even over other constitutional statutes. R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the EU (2017) treated the ECA 1972 as having constitutional character.

Arguments about codification
For: clarity, accessibility, entrenched rights and a check on a strong executive. Against: rigidity, a shift of power to judges, and the difficulty of agreeing the content.

Worked illustration
Is the convention that the monarch acts on prime ministerial advice 'law'? No: it is a convention. A court would acknowledge it but would not order the monarch to comply. In Miller (2017) the Sewel Convention was held not to be legally enforceable even after its recognition in statute.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying the UK has an 'unwritten' constitution; most of it is written, just not in one document.
- Treating conventions as legally enforceable.
- Ignoring the difference between legal and political constitutionalism when evaluating.

Dicey: Parliament (King, Lords and Commons) can make or unmake any law, and no person or body may override or set aside its legislation.

Components
- No limit on subject matter: the War Damage Act 1965 retrospectively reversed Burmah Oil v Lord Advocate (1965); conventions do not limit legislative power (Madzimbamuto v Lardner-Burke 1969).
- Courts will not look behind an Act's passage (the enrolled Act rule: Pickin v British Railways Board 1974; also Bill of Rights 1689 art 9).
- Implied repeal: a later inconsistent Act prevails (Vauxhall Estates v Liverpool Corporation 1932; Ellen Street Estates v Minister of Health 1934).
- Parliament cannot bind its successors.

Challenges
- Manner and form theory: Parliament may be able to redefine the procedure for legislating (AG for New South Wales v Trethowan 1932; Jennings). Jackson v AG (2005) upheld the Hunting Act 2004, passed under the Parliament Acts, and confirmed that the 1911 Act's procedure creates primary legislation. Obiter, Lords Steyn and Hope and Baroness Hale suggested courts might decline to uphold legislation abolishing judicial review or fundamental rights.
- EU membership: Factortame (No 2) (1991) disapplied an Act of Parliament inconsistent with directly effective EU law, explained as Parliament's own choice through the ECA 1972. This largely ended with Brexit: from 1 January 2024 the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 provides that the principle of supremacy of EU law is not part of domestic law (EUWA 2018 s5(A1)). That is subject to 'relevant separation agreement law' (s5(7)). Under EUWA s7A, directly effective provisions of the Withdrawal Agreement, including the Windsor Framework, still prevail over inconsistent Acts. In Re Dillon the Northern Ireland courts used this in 2024 to disapply parts of the Legacy Act 2023, but the Supreme Court set those orders aside in 2026 ([2026] UKSC 15) because no directly effective EU right had been breached.
- Human Rights Act 1998: courts interpret statutes compatibly where possible (s3) but can only declare incompatibility (s4); they cannot strike down Acts.
- Common law constitutionalism: the principle of legality presumes that general words do not override fundamental rights (R v Home Secretary, ex p Simms 2000). R (Privacy International) v Investigatory Powers Tribunal (2019) read down an apparent ouster clause, with Lord Carnwath suggesting obiter that it is ultimately for the courts to determine the limits Parliament may place on judicial review.

Theories
Wade saw sovereignty as a political fact, the ultimate rule of recognition, changeable only by a judicial 'revolution' (perhaps Factortame). Jennings and Heuston's 'new view' allows procedural self-limitation.

Worked illustration
A 2026 Act states 'This Act may not be repealed except with a two-thirds majority in the Commons'. On orthodox Diceyan theory a later Act passed by simple majority would impliedly repeal it. On manner and form theory a court might insist on the special procedure. The point is unresolved in UK law.

Exam pitfalls
- Stating that Jackson decided Parliament's power is limited; the limits were obiter.
- Forgetting that the HRA preserves sovereignty.
- Treating Factortame as still describing the post-Brexit position, or forgetting the narrow s7A exception for the Windsor Framework.

notes.h: Rule of law and separation of powers
notes.body:
Rule of law
- Dicey: no punishment except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary courts; equality before the law, including officials; and constitutional rights deriving from ordinary judicial decisions.
- Raz: a formal conception (laws prospective, open, clear and stable; independent, accessible courts). Bingham's The Rule of Law (2010) gave eight principles, including protection of fundamental rights and compliance with international law: a 'thicker' conception.
- Statutory recognition: the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 s1 preserves 'the existing constitutional principle of the rule of law', and s3 imposes a duty on ministers to uphold judicial independence.

Key cases
- Entick v Carrington (1765): officials must show lawful authority for interfering with property.
- M v Home Office (1994): ministers can be held in contempt of court.
- Anisminic v FCC (1969): an ouster clause did not protect a decision vitiated by error of law, which was a nullity.
- R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor (2017): employment tribunal fees preventing access to justice were unlawful; access to the courts is inherent in the rule of law.
- R (Evans) v AG (2015): overriding a judicial decision by ministerial veto needs crystal clear statutory words.

Separation of powers
Montesquieu argued liberty requires legislative, executive and judicial functions to be held separately. The UK has a partial separation with checks and balances:
- Executive and legislature overlap: ministers sit in Parliament (at most 95 in the Commons: House of Commons Disqualification Act 1975).
- The judiciary has been separated more firmly by the CRA 2005, which created the Supreme Court (in operation from 2009), reformed the Lord Chancellor's role and established the Judicial Appointments Commission.
- Courts respect Parliament's sphere through parliamentary privilege and the enrolled Act rule, and the executive's sphere through deference on policy (R (Begum) v SIAC 2021).
- Courts police executive encroachment on Parliament: Miller II (2019) held a five-week prorogation unlawful.
- R v Home Secretary, ex p Fire Brigades Union (1995): a minister could not use the prerogative to frustrate a statutory scheme Parliament had enacted.

The Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 inserted s29A into the Senior Courts Act 1981 (suspended and prospective quashing orders) and reversed Cart (2011) by ousting judicial review of Upper Tribunal refusals of permission to appeal, subject to exceptions.

Worked illustration
A minister announces a policy that removes rights granted by statute. Fire Brigades Union shows the prerogative cannot be used to undermine Parliament's choice; Entick requires positive authority for coercive action.

Exam pitfalls
- Defining the rule of law only by Dicey without engaging formal and substantive views.
- Claiming the UK has a strict separation of powers.
- Ignoring the 2022 Act when discussing ouster clauses.

The executive comprises the Crown, the Prime Minister and Cabinet, ministers and departments, the civil service and executive agencies. The Prime Minister holds office by convention, as the person best able to command the confidence of the House of Commons.

The royal prerogative
Dicey called it 'the residue of discretionary or arbitrary authority' legally left in the Crown's hands. Examples include conducting foreign affairs and making treaties, deploying the armed forces, granting honours, the prerogative of mercy, issuing passports, appointing ministers and proroguing Parliament.
- No new prerogatives can be created (BBC v Johns 1965).
- The prerogative cannot change domestic law (Case of Proclamations 1610) or be used to alter rights conferred by statute (Miller I 2017).
- Statute displaces overlapping prerogative while it is in force (AG v De Keyser's Royal Hotel 1920; Laker Airways v Department of Trade 1977).
- The courts decide whether a prerogative exists and its extent (Case of Proclamations; Miller II 2019).

Statutory reform
- Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 Part 2 put the Ponsonby Rule on a statutory basis: a treaty is laid before Parliament for 21 sitting days before ratification, and the Commons can delay it.
- The Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011 removed the dissolution prerogative; the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 repealed it, revived the prerogative and in s3 purports to oust judicial review of it. Parliament dissolves automatically five years after first meeting.

Judicial review of the prerogative
CCSU v Minister for the Civil Service (1985) held that the source of a power does not matter; reviewability depends on its subject matter. Some matters, such as treaty-making, defence, honours and dissolution, were considered unsuitable. Later cases reviewed mercy (R v Home Secretary, ex p Bentley 1994) and passports (ex p Everett 1989).

Conventions
Conventions are non-legal rules regarded as binding by those to whom they apply (Dicey). Jennings asked: are there precedents; do the actors believe they are bound; is there a reason for the rule? Examples include collective and individual ministerial responsibility, royal assent and the Sewel Convention. Courts may recognise conventions but will not enforce them (AG v Jonathan Cape 1976; Madzimbamuto; Miller I). The Ministerial Code and Cabinet Manual record many of them.

Worked illustration
A government may ratify a trade treaty by prerogative, subject to CRAG 2010 Part 2, but any change to domestic law needed to implement it requires an Act.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying all prerogative powers are unreviewable; CCSU shifted the focus to justiciability.
- Assuming statutory recognition of a convention makes it legally enforceable.
- Forgetting that the 2022 Act revived the prerogative of dissolution.

Devolution transfers power to elected institutions in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland while Parliament remains sovereign: the UK is a union state, not a federation.

Scotland
- Scotland Act 1998: the Scottish Parliament can legislate on anything not reserved (a reserved powers model). Section 29 sets the limits on its competence, including reserved matters in Schedule 5, Convention rights and the protected enactments in Schedule 4. Section 28(7) preserves Westminster's power to legislate for Scotland.
- The Scotland Act 2016 added s63A (the Scottish Parliament and Government are permanent parts of the UK constitution and not to be abolished except after a referendum) and s28(8) (recognising the Sewel Convention).
- Reference on the UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Bill (2021): provisions that would have qualified Westminster's continuing power to legislate for Scotland were outside competence.
- Reference re Scottish Independence Referendum Bill (2022): a Bill for an advisory independence referendum related to reserved matters (the Union and the UK Parliament) and was outside competence.
- In 2023 the UK Government first used s35 to block a Bill (Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill); the Court of Session upheld the order.

Wales
The Senedd moved from executive devolution (Government of Wales Act 1998) to primary law-making after the 2011 referendum, and to a reserved powers model (Wales Act 2017). The Senedd Cymru (Members and Elections) Act 2024 enlarged it to 96 members, elected by closed list proportional representation from May 2026.

Northern Ireland
The Northern Ireland Act 1998 implements the Belfast/Good Friday Agreement 1998, with power-sharing between unionist and nationalist parties, cross-community voting and transferred, reserved and excepted matters. In Re Allister (2023) the Supreme Court held that the Northern Ireland Protocol arrangements (later amended and renamed the Windsor Framework) lawfully modified the Acts of Union through the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 s7A.

England
There is no English Parliament. 'English votes for English laws' (2015) was abolished in 2021. Combined authorities and metro mayors provide limited regional devolution.

Intergovernmental relations
The Sewel Convention: Westminster will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the consent of the devolved legislature. In Miller I (2017) the Supreme Court held it a political convention, not enforceable in court. The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 was passed without Scottish consent. The United Kingdom Internal Market Act 2020 created market access principles that devolved administrations argue constrain their powers.

Worked illustration
A Scottish Bill regulating broadcasting relates to a reserved matter (Schedule 5), so is outside competence under s29 and 'not law'; the law officers could refer it to the Supreme Court under s33 before royal assent.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying devolved legislatures are sovereign.
- Treating s63A as legal entrenchment; Westminster's power remains.
- Treating Sewel as legally enforceable.

Judicial review is the High Court's supervision of the lawfulness, not the merits, of public decisions.

Procedure
- Senior Courts Act 1981 s31 and CPR Part 54; permission is required.
- Time limit: promptly and in any event within three months of the grounds arising (CPR 54.5), or six weeks in planning cases.
- Standing: 'sufficient interest' (s31(3); IRC v National Federation of Self-Employed 1982), generously applied to campaign groups (ex p World Development Movement 1995).
- Amenability: public bodies and those performing public functions (R v Panel on Take-overs and Mergers, ex p Datafin 1987); contractual or consensual bodies are excluded (R v Disciplinary Committee of the Jockey Club, ex p Aga Khan 1993).
- Relief must be refused if the outcome would highly likely not have been substantially different (s31(2A)).
- Remedies: quashing (including suspended or prospective, s29A), mandatory and prohibiting orders, declarations and injunctions.

Grounds: Lord Diplock in CCSU (1985)
1. Illegality: the decision-maker must understand and give effect to the law. This covers errors of law (Anisminic 1969), improper purpose (Padfield v Minister of Agriculture 1968; Porter v Magill 2001), relevant and irrelevant considerations (R v Somerset CC, ex p Fewings 1995), fettering discretion (British Oxygen v Board of Trade 1971) and unlawful delegation (contrast Carltona 1943 for officials acting for ministers).
2. Irrationality: a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it (Associated Provincial Picture Houses v Wednesbury 1948). Scrutiny intensifies where fundamental rights are engaged (R v Ministry of Defence, ex p Smith 1996; Pham v Home Secretary 2015).
3. Procedural impropriety: breach of statutory procedure; the right to a fair hearing (Ridge v Baldwin 1964; R v Home Secretary, ex p Doody 1994); and the rule against bias, judged by whether the fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias (Porter v Magill 2001), with automatic disqualification for interest (Dimes 1852; Pinochet (No 2) 2000).
4. Legitimate expectation: procedural or substantive, arising from a clear and unambiguous promise or practice (ex p Coughlan 2001); frustrating it must be proportionate (Re Finucane 2019).
5. Proportionality: required under the HRA, applying Bank Mellat v HM Treasury (No 2) (2013). It is not a general common law ground (R (Keyu) v Foreign Secretary 2015).

Worked illustration
A council refuses a trader's licence renewal without disclosing the objections: procedural impropriety, since he should have a chance to respond (Doody). A rigid rule never to renew for anyone over 70 would also fetter discretion.

Exam pitfalls
- Arguing the merits rather than legality.
- Forgetting permission, standing and time limits in a problem question.
- Treating proportionality as an established common law ground.

The Human Rights Act 1998 gives domestic effect to most ECHR rights (Schedule 1) while preserving parliamentary sovereignty.

Key provisions
- s2: courts must take into account Strasbourg case law. They normally follow clear and constant Strasbourg jurisprudence (R (Ullah) v Special Adjudicator 2004), may decline to do so (R v Horncastle 2009), and should not normally go further than Strasbourg has gone (R (AB) v Justice Secretary 2021).
- s3: legislation must be read and given effect compatibly 'so far as it is possible to do so'. This is a strong obligation (Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza 2004: reading 'as his or her wife or husband' to include same-sex partners), but it cannot go against the grain of the legislation (Re S (Care Order) 2002).
- s4: if a compatible reading is impossible, a higher court can make a declaration of incompatibility (Bellinger v Bellinger 2003; R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice 2014 on the court's discretion). The declaration does not affect the validity of the Act (s4(6)).
- s6: it is unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with Convention rights. Core public authorities are always bound; 'hybrid' bodies are bound when performing functions of a public nature (Aston Cantlow PCC v Wallbank 2003; YL v Birmingham CC 2007, reversed for publicly arranged care by the Care Act 2014 s73; R (Weaver) v London & Quadrant Housing Trust 2009). Courts are public authorities, giving the Act some horizontal effect.
- s7: only a 'victim' may sue, usually within one year.
- s8: damages where necessary for just satisfaction.
- s10: a minister can make a remedial order after a declaration of incompatibility.
- s19: ministers make a statement of compatibility for Bills.

Structure of rights
- Absolute: Article 3. Limited: Articles 5 and 6.
- Qualified rights: Articles 8 to 11, which may be restricted if prescribed by law, in pursuit of a legitimate aim and necessary in a democratic society. Necessity is tested by proportionality (Bank Mellat 2013): a sufficiently important objective, a rational connection, no less intrusive measure, and a fair balance.

Reform
The Bill of Rights Bill (2022), which would have repealed and replaced the HRA, was withdrawn in 2023. As of 2026 the HRA remains in force.

Worked illustration
A statute requires a landlord to evict 'any occupier'. If eviction would disproportionately interfere with Article 8, the court first tries a compatible reading under s3; if that is impossible, it may declare incompatibility under s4, but must still apply the statute.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying courts can strike down Acts under the HRA.
- Treating s2 as requiring courts to follow Strasbourg.
- Applying s6 to private bodies without analysing public functions.

Key stages
- European Union Referendum Act 2015: the 2016 referendum was advisory in law.
- R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the EU (2017) (Miller I): notifying withdrawal under Article 50 TEU by prerogative would remove rights given by the ECA 1972 and change domestic law, so an Act was needed. The European Union (Notification of Withdrawal) Act 2017 followed. The Sewel Convention was held non-justiciable.
- R (Miller) v Prime Minister; Cherry v Advocate General (2019) (Miller II): the prorogation decision was justiciable and unlawful because it frustrated Parliament's ability to carry out its constitutional functions without reasonable justification; it was treated as null.
- The European Union (Withdrawal Agreement) Act 2020 implemented the Withdrawal Agreement. The UK left on 31 January 2020; the transition period ended on 31 December 2020.

The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018
- Repealed the ECA 1972 (s1) and converted existing EU-derived law into 'retained EU law' (ss2–4).
- Section 7A, inserted by the European Union (Withdrawal Agreement) Act 2020, gave effect to the Withdrawal Agreement, including the Northern Ireland Protocol, with priority over inconsistent domestic law.
- Section 8 gave ministers wide 'Henry VIII' powers to correct deficiencies, raising rule of law and accountability concerns.

Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023
- Renamed retained EU law as 'assimilated law' from 1 January 2024.
- Abolished the principle of supremacy of EU law and general principles of EU law for that law, and revoked listed instruments. This is subject to Withdrawal Agreement law given effect by s7A (EUWA 2018 s5(7)).

Northern Ireland
The Protocol kept Northern Ireland aligned with many EU single market rules for goods to avoid a land border. The Windsor Framework (2023) amended it, including the Stormont Brake. Re Allister (2023) held that the Protocol arrangements lawfully modified Article VI of the Act of Union 1800, applying ordinary sovereignty principles. Article 2(1) of the Windsor Framework commits the UK to ensure no diminution of the rights, safeguards and equality of opportunity in the relevant chapter of the Belfast/Good Friday Agreement resulting from withdrawal, including the anti-discrimination protections in the directives listed in Annex 1. In Re Dillon the NI High Court (2024) and Court of Appeal ([2024] NICA 59) disapplied the Legacy Act 2023's immunity provisions under Article 2 and s7A. The Supreme Court reversed this ([2026] UKSC 15). It accepted that Article 2 can have direct effect in limited cases, for example together with an Annex 1 directive, but held that no directly effective EU right was breached: the Victims' Directive does not regulate a statutory immunity scheme. Separate HRA declarations of incompatibility about the Act were not appealed and still stand.

Constitutional lessons
- Sovereignty was largely reasserted: Factortame-style disapplication for EU law has ended, except where s7A gives priority to directly effective Withdrawal Agreement or Windsor Framework provisions, a route the Supreme Court in Re Dillon (2026) confined narrowly.
- The referendum created political, not legal, obligations.
- The courts became more willing to protect Parliament's role against the executive (Miller I and II), prompting debate about judicial power and the 2022 reforms.
- Devolution strains: Sewel was overridden, and the Internal Market Act 2020 recentralised some power.

Worked illustration
Is a 2019 EU regulation still binding in the UK? If it applied before 31 December 2020, it became retained EU law and, after the 2023 Act, assimilated law. It can now be amended domestically, and EU supremacy no longer applies to it.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying Miller I decided Brexit could not happen without parliamentary approval of the result; it concerned the method of Article 50 notification.
- Overlooking the Northern Ireland dimension.
- Describing post-2024 law as 'retained EU law' instead of 'assimilated law'.

cards.f: Why is the UK constitution described as 'uncodified' rather than 'unwritten'?
cards.b: Most of it is written, in statutes, cases and official documents, but it is not collected in a single supreme constitutional text.

cards.f: Name four sources of the UK constitution.
cards.b: Statute, common law, constitutional conventions, and the law and custom of Parliament; authoritative works and soft-law documents such as the Cabinet Manual are also relevant.

cards.f: What is a constitutional convention?
cards.b: A non-legal rule of constitutional behaviour that those it applies to regard as binding, such as the monarch granting royal assent to Bills passed by Parliament.

cards.f: What did Laws LJ suggest in Thoburn v Sunderland CC (2002)?
cards.b: That 'constitutional statutes', such as the ECA 1972 and the Human Rights Act, cannot be impliedly repealed and can be repealed only by express words or unavoidably clear language.

cards.f: What is the significance of R (HS2 Action Alliance) v Transport Secretary (2014)?
cards.b: The Supreme Court suggested that fundamental constitutional principles, such as those in the Bill of Rights 1689 art 9, might prevail even over another constitutional statute like the ECA 1972.

cards.f: Distinguish political from legal constitutionalism.
cards.b: Political constitutionalism relies on Parliament, elections and political accountability to check government (Griffith). Legal constitutionalism emphasises courts enforcing fundamental values and limits on power (Allan).

cards.f: Give two arguments for codifying the UK constitution.
cards.b: Greater clarity and accessibility for citizens; and entrenched protection of rights and limits on a powerful executive that commands a Commons majority.

cards.f: Give two arguments against codification.
cards.b: It would reduce flexibility and the ability to evolve through convention; and it would transfer power over contested political questions to unelected judges.

cards.f: Did statutory recognition make the Sewel Convention legally enforceable?
cards.b: No. In Miller I (2017) the Supreme Court held that the Scotland Act 1998 s28(8) recognised the convention as political and did not convert it into a legal rule.

cards.f: State Dicey's definition of parliamentary sovereignty.
cards.b: Parliament has the right to make or unmake any law whatever, and no person or body is recognised by law as having a right to override or set aside its legislation.

cards.f: What is the doctrine of implied repeal?
cards.b: Where a later Act is inconsistent with an earlier one, the later Act prevails to the extent of the inconsistency (Vauxhall Estates 1932; Ellen Street Estates 1934).

cards.f: What is the enrolled Act rule? Give the authority.
cards.b: Courts will not inquire into the parliamentary procedure by which an Act was passed (Pickin v British Railways Board 1974).

cards.f: What did Jackson v AG (2005) decide?
cards.b: The Hunting Act 2004 and the Parliament Act 1949 were valid; legislation passed under the Parliament Acts procedure is primary legislation.

cards.f: What obiter comments in Jackson challenged orthodox sovereignty?
cards.b: Lords Steyn and Hope and Baroness Hale suggested courts might refuse to give effect to an Act abolishing judicial review or fundamental rights, with Lord Steyn describing sovereignty as a construct of the common law.

cards.f: What happened in Factortame (No 2) (1991)?
cards.b: The House of Lords disapplied the Merchant Shipping Act 1988 because it conflicted with directly effective EU law, giving effect to the ECA 1972.

cards.f: What is the 'manner and form' theory?
cards.b: The view that Parliament can redefine the procedure or form required for valid legislation, binding future Parliaments to follow it (Jennings; AG for New South Wales v Trethowan 1932).

cards.f: What is the principle of legality?
cards.b: A presumption that Parliament does not intend general words to override fundamental rights; express language or necessary implication is required (R v Home Secretary, ex p Simms 2000).

cards.f: What did Lord Carnwath suggest in R (Privacy International) v IPT (2019)?
cards.b: Obiter, that it is ultimately for the courts, not Parliament, to determine the extent to which judicial review can be excluded, and that binding effect may be denied to a clause purporting to oust review of errors of law.

cards.f: How did Wade explain Factortame?
cards.b: As a 'revolution': a change in the ultimate rule of recognition, since Parliament had effectively bound its successors.

cards.f: State Dicey's three principles of the rule of law.
cards.b: No punishment except for a distinct breach of law established before the ordinary courts; equality of all, including officials, before the ordinary law; and constitutional rights resulting from ordinary judicial decisions.

cards.f: Distinguish formal and substantive conceptions of the rule of law.
cards.b: Formal conceptions (Raz) concern the qualities of law, such as clarity, prospectivity and stability. Substantive conceptions (Bingham) also require protection of fundamental rights.

cards.f: What is the principle in Entick v Carrington (1765)?
cards.b: State officials must show positive legal authority for interfering with a person's property; general warrants were unlawful.

cards.f: What did M v Home Office (1994) establish?
cards.b: Ministers and government departments are subject to the courts' jurisdiction and can be found in contempt.

cards.f: What was decided in R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor (2017)?
cards.b: Employment tribunal fees were unlawful because they effectively prevented access to justice, which is inherent in the rule of law.

cards.f: Which statute contains a statutory reference to the rule of law?
cards.b: The Constitutional Reform Act 2005 s1, which preserves the existing constitutional principle of the rule of law and the Lord Chancellor's role in relation to it.

cards.f: What three reforms did the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 make to separation of powers?
cards.b: It created the Supreme Court, removed the Lord Chancellor's judicial role and role as Speaker of the Lords, and established the Judicial Appointments Commission.

cards.f: What principle came from R v Home Secretary, ex p Fire Brigades Union (1995)?
cards.b: A minister could not use prerogative power to introduce a scheme inconsistent with a statutory scheme Parliament had enacted but not yet brought into force.

cards.f: What changes did the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 make?
cards.b: It enabled suspended and prospective quashing orders (SCA 1981 s29A) and ousted judicial review of Upper Tribunal refusals of permission to appeal, reversing Cart (2011) subject to exceptions.

cards.f: What did Anisminic v FCC (1969) decide about ouster clauses?
cards.b: A clause protecting 'determinations' did not protect a purported determination vitiated by an error of law, which was a nullity.

cards.f: Define the royal prerogative.
cards.b: The residue of discretionary or arbitrary authority legally left in the hands of the Crown (Dicey); powers recognised by common law rather than statute.

cards.f: Give four examples of prerogative powers.
cards.b: Making treaties, deploying the armed forces, granting honours, issuing passports, the prerogative of mercy, and appointing ministers.

cards.f: What is the rule in De Keyser's Royal Hotel (1920)?
cards.b: Where statute covers the same ground as a prerogative power, the prerogative is placed in abeyance and the government must act under the statute.

cards.f: What did CCSU v Minister for the Civil Service (1985) decide about the prerogative?
cards.b: Prerogative powers are reviewable in principle; reviewability depends on subject matter rather than source. Some areas, such as national security, treaties and honours, were considered non-justiciable.

cards.f: What did the Case of Proclamations (1610) establish?
cards.b: The King cannot change the law of the land by proclamation; the Crown has only the prerogative powers the law allows.

cards.f: What did the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 do?
cards.b: It repealed the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011, revived the prerogative to dissolve Parliament, sought to exclude judicial review of dissolution (s3), and provided for automatic dissolution five years after Parliament first meets.

cards.f: What does Part 2 of CRAG 2010 provide?
cards.b: A treaty must be laid before Parliament for 21 sitting days before ratification; if the Commons resolves against it, the government must explain and the period can be extended.

cards.f: State the convention of collective ministerial responsibility.
cards.b: Ministers must publicly support government decisions, keep Cabinet discussions confidential, and the government must resign or seek dissolution if it loses the confidence of the Commons.

cards.f: What did AG v Jonathan Cape (1976) show about conventions?
cards.b: The court would not enforce the convention of Cabinet confidentiality as such, but could restrain publication through the law of confidence; by then the material was too old to restrain.

cards.f: State Jennings's test for the existence of a convention.
cards.b: Are there precedents? Do the actors believe they are bound by a rule? Is there a reason for the rule?

cards.f: What legislative model does the Scotland Act 1998 adopt?
cards.b: A reserved powers model: the Scottish Parliament may legislate on anything not reserved to Westminster or otherwise outside competence under s29.

cards.f: What limits on legislative competence are in Scotland Act 1998 s29?
cards.b: Provisions are outside competence if they relate to reserved matters, breach Convention rights, modify protected enactments in Schedule 4, or apply outside Scotland, among others.

cards.f: What does Scotland Act 1998 s28(7) provide?
cards.b: That the Scottish Parliament's power to make laws does not affect the power of the UK Parliament to make laws for Scotland.

cards.f: What is the Sewel Convention?
cards.b: Westminster will not normally legislate with regard to devolved matters without the consent of the devolved legislature.

cards.f: What did the Supreme Court decide in the Scottish Independence Referendum Bill reference (2022)?
cards.b: Even an advisory referendum on independence related to reserved matters (the Union and the UK Parliament), so the Bill was outside the Scottish Parliament's competence.

cards.f: What did the UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Bill reference (2021) decide?
cards.b: Provisions that would have restricted the effect of Westminster legislation for Scotland were outside competence because they modified s28(7) of the Scotland Act.

cards.f: What is s35 of the Scotland Act 1998 and when was it first used?
cards.b: It lets the Secretary of State block a Bill from royal assent on specified grounds, including adverse effects on reserved law. It was first used in 2023 for the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill.

cards.f: What model of devolution has Wales had since the Wales Act 2017?
cards.b: A reserved powers model like Scotland's, replacing the earlier conferred powers model.

cards.f: What is the constitutional basis of Northern Ireland's devolved institutions?
cards.b: The Northern Ireland Act 1998, implementing the Belfast/Good Friday Agreement 1998, with compulsory power-sharing and transferred, reserved and excepted matters.

cards.f: What did Re Allister (2023) decide?
cards.b: The Protocol arrangements, given effect by EUWA 2018 s7A, lawfully modified Article VI of the Act of Union 1800; the s1 Northern Ireland Act consent principle concerns constitutional status, not trade, so was not breached.

cards.f: What is the time limit for judicial review?
cards.b: Promptly and in any event within three months of the grounds first arising (CPR 54.5), with shorter periods in planning and procurement cases.

cards.f: What is the standing test for judicial review?
cards.b: A 'sufficient interest' in the matter (Senior Courts Act 1981 s31(3); IRC v National Federation of Self-Employed 1982).

cards.f: What did R v Panel on Take-overs, ex p Datafin (1987) decide?
cards.b: A body without statutory or prerogative powers can be amenable to judicial review if it performs public functions.

cards.f: Name Lord Diplock's three grounds of review in CCSU.
cards.b: Illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety, with proportionality noted as a possible future ground.

cards.f: What is Wednesbury unreasonableness?
cards.b: A decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could ever have come to it (Associated Provincial Picture Houses v Wednesbury 1948).

cards.f: What is the test for apparent bias?
cards.b: Whether the fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, would conclude there was a real possibility that the tribunal was biased (Porter v Magill 2001).

cards.f: What does fettering discretion mean?
cards.b: Adopting a rigid policy that prevents consideration of individual cases. A policy is allowed if the decision-maker is willing to hear exceptions (British Oxygen v Board of Trade 1971).

cards.f: When can a substantive legitimate expectation be enforced?
cards.b: Where a clear, unambiguous and unqualified promise was made, and frustrating it would be so unfair as to amount to an abuse of power, as in ex p Coughlan (2001); the authority must show a proportionate justification.

cards.f: What does Senior Courts Act 1981 s31(2A) require?
cards.b: The court must refuse relief if it appears highly likely that the outcome for the applicant would not have been substantially different had the conduct complained of not occurred, unless there is exceptional public interest.

cards.f: What did Padfield v Minister of Agriculture (1968) decide?
cards.b: A minister's discretion must be used to promote the policy and objects of the Act; refusing to refer a complaint for reasons that frustrated the statute's purpose was unlawful.

cards.f: What does s3 of the Human Rights Act 1998 require?
cards.b: So far as it is possible to do so, primary and subordinate legislation must be read and given effect in a way compatible with Convention rights.

cards.f: What is the effect of a s4 declaration of incompatibility?
cards.b: It does not affect the validity, continuing operation or enforcement of the legislation (s4(6)); it signals the incompatibility to Parliament and the government.

cards.f: What did Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza (2004) decide?
cards.b: Under s3 the Rent Act phrase 'as his or her wife or husband' was read to include same-sex partners; s3 can require departure from the ordinary meaning if this does not go against the grain of the legislation.

cards.f: What does HRA s6 provide?
cards.b: It is unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with a Convention right, unless primary legislation requires it to do so.

cards.f: What did YL v Birmingham CC (2007) decide, and how was it reversed?
cards.b: A private care home providing publicly funded care was not performing a public function under s6(3)(b). Care Act 2014 s73 reversed this for regulated care arranged or funded by a local authority.

cards.f: What does s2 HRA require of courts?
cards.b: They must take into account Strasbourg judgments and decisions, but are not bound to follow them.

cards.f: State the Bank Mellat (No 2) (2013) proportionality test.
cards.b: Is the objective sufficiently important? Is the measure rationally connected to it? Could a less intrusive measure have been used without unacceptably compromising the objective? Does the measure strike a fair balance between the individual and the community?

cards.f: Give an example of an absolute and a qualified right.
cards.b: Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) is absolute; Article 8 (private and family life) is qualified.

cards.f: What happened to the Bill of Rights Bill 2022?
cards.b: It was withdrawn in 2023 without being enacted, so the Human Rights Act 1998 remains in force.

cards.f: Who can bring proceedings under HRA s7?
cards.b: Only a person who is, or would be, a victim of the unlawful act within the meaning of Article 34 ECHR.

cards.f: What did Miller I (2017) decide?
cards.b: Notice of withdrawal under Article 50 TEU required an Act of Parliament because it would remove rights given by the ECA 1972 and change domestic law; the prerogative could not do this.

cards.f: What did Miller II / Cherry (2019) decide?
cards.b: The prorogation advice was justiciable and unlawful because it frustrated, without reasonable justification, Parliament's ability to carry out its constitutional functions; the prorogation was void.

cards.f: When did the UK leave the EU and when did the transition period end?
cards.b: The UK left on 31 January 2020; the transition period ended at 11pm on 31 December 2020.

cards.f: What did the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 do with EU law?
cards.b: It repealed the ECA 1972 and preserved most EU-derived law on exit day as 'retained EU law', giving ministers powers to correct deficiencies.

cards.f: What did the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 do?
cards.b: It renamed retained EU law as 'assimilated law' from 2024, abolished EU supremacy and general principles for that law, and revoked many instruments. This is subject to Withdrawal Agreement law under EUWA s7A.

cards.f: What is a Henry VIII power, and why does EUWA 2018 s8 raise concerns?
cards.b: A power allowing ministers to amend or repeal primary legislation by secondary legislation. Section 8 is broad, reducing parliamentary scrutiny.

cards.f: What is the Stormont Brake?
cards.b: A Windsor Framework (2023) mechanism allowing 30 MLAs from at least two parties to trigger a process through which the UK may prevent amended EU goods rules applying in Northern Ireland.

cards.f: How did Brexit test the Sewel Convention?
cards.b: The Scottish Parliament refused consent to the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018 and later Brexit legislation, but Westminster legislated anyway, showing the convention's political rather than legal force.

cards.f: What constitutional role did the 2016 referendum play?
cards.b: It was advisory in law under the European Union Referendum Act 2015, but created strong political obligations; legal effect required further Acts of Parliament.

cards.f: Why was EUWA 2018 s7A important?
cards.b: It gave domestic effect to the Withdrawal Agreement, including the Northern Ireland Protocol, with priority over inconsistent domestic law, as a Factortame-like mechanism. In Re Dillon [2026] UKSC 15 the Supreme Court held it only bites where a provision is directly effective under EU law, and set aside the NI courts' disapplication of the Legacy Act 2023.

questions.q: Which best describes the UK constitution?
options: Codified and rigid
Uncodified and largely flexible
Codified but flexible
Federal and entrenched
questions.why: The UK has no single constitutional document and most constitutional rules can be changed by ordinary Act of Parliament.

questions.q: Which case confirmed that courts will not investigate the procedure by which an Act was passed?
options: Jackson v AG (2005)
Pickin v British Railways Board (1974)
Factortame (No 2) (1991)
Thoburn v Sunderland CC (2002)
questions.why: Pickin established the enrolled Act rule: courts look only at the Parliament roll, not at internal parliamentary procedure.

questions.q: Which case held employment tribunal fees unlawful as an obstacle to access to justice?
options: R (Evans) v AG (2015)
R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor (2017)
M v Home Office (1994)
Anisminic v FCC (1969)
questions.why: UNISON treated access to courts as inherent in the rule of law, and the fees order was quashed.

questions.q: According to AG v De Keyser's Royal Hotel (1920), what happens when statute covers the same ground as a prerogative power?
options: The prerogative and statute run in parallel
The prerogative is abolished permanently
The prerogative is placed in abeyance and the Crown must act under the statute
The Crown may choose which to use
questions.why: Statute displaces overlapping prerogative while the statute is in force, so the executive must use the statutory power.

questions.q: Under the Scotland Act 1998, what is the legal status of an Act of the Scottish Parliament that relates to a reserved matter?
options: Valid until repealed by Westminster
Valid but subject to a declaration of incompatibility
Not law, so far as outside legislative competence
Valid if the Sewel Convention was followed
questions.why: Section 29(1) provides that a provision outside legislative competence is not law.

questions.q: What is the usual time limit for bringing a claim for judicial review?
options: Six years
Promptly and in any event within three months
One year
28 days
questions.why: CPR 54.5 requires claims to be filed promptly and in any event within three months after the grounds first arose.

questions.q: What is the legal effect of a declaration of incompatibility under s4 HRA 1998?
options: The Act is void
The Act is suspended until Parliament acts
The Act remains valid and enforceable
The minister must amend the Act within six months
questions.why: Section 4(6) states the declaration does not affect the validity, continuing operation or enforcement of the provision.

questions.q: Why did Miller I (2017) require an Act of Parliament for notification under Article 50?
options: Because the referendum result was legally binding
Because withdrawal would change domestic law and remove statutory rights, which the prerogative cannot do
Because the Sewel Convention required devolved consent
Because Article 50 itself requires a parliamentary vote
questions.why: The prerogative cannot alter domestic law or remove rights given by statute; the ECA 1972 had made EU law a source of domestic law.

questions.q: Which statement about the rule against bias is correct?
options: Actual bias must always be proved
The test for apparent bias is whether the fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias
A pecuniary interest disqualifies only if it influenced the decision
Bias applies only to judges, not administrative decision-makers
questions.why: Porter v Magill (2001) set the fair-minded and informed observer test; financial interests lead to automatic disqualification regardless of influence.

questions.q: Which statement about Jackson v AG (2005) is accurate?
options: It held that Parliament's power to abolish judicial review is legally limited
It held that the Parliament Act 1949 was invalid
It upheld the Hunting Act 2004, with obiter remarks questioning absolute sovereignty
It held that Acts passed under the Parliament Acts are delegated legislation
questions.why: The ratio upheld the 1949 Act and the Hunting Act as primary legislation; comments on limits to sovereignty were obiter.

questions.q: Which body is most likely a 'hybrid' public authority under HRA s6(3)(b)?
options: A government department
A private housing association performing allocation and management of social housing
A purely commercial supermarket
A local authority
questions.why: In Weaver (2009) a housing association's management of social housing was a public function; departments and councils are core public authorities.

questions.q: Explain what constitutional conventions are and why courts do not enforce them.
markScheme: Non-legal rules regarded as binding by those to whom they apply
Example, e.g. royal assent, ministerial responsibility, Sewel
Courts may recognise but not enforce (Jonathan Cape; Madzimbamuto)
Miller I: political in nature; enforcement through political process
questions.modelAnswer: Conventions are non-legal rules of political behaviour which those to whom they apply regard as binding, such as the convention that the monarch grants royal assent to Bills passed by Parliament. They regulate how legal powers are exercised. Courts may recognise conventions and use them in interpreting law, but will not enforce them directly (AG v Jonathan Cape 1976; Madzimbamuto 1969). In Miller I (2017) the Supreme Court said conventions operate in the political world, so their enforcement is a matter for politicians and the electorate, not judges.

questions.q: Explain the doctrine of implied repeal and how the 'constitutional statutes' idea qualifies it.
markScheme: Later inconsistent Act prevails over earlier to the extent of inconsistency
Vauxhall Estates; Ellen Street Estates
Thoburn: constitutional statutes not impliedly repealed
Need express words or unavoidable implication
Status contested; HS2 suggests a hierarchy of constitutional principles
questions.modelAnswer: Implied repeal means that if a later Act is inconsistent with an earlier one, the later Act prevails to the extent of the inconsistency, even without express repeal (Vauxhall Estates 1932; Ellen Street Estates 1934). It follows from the principle that Parliament cannot bind its successors. In Thoburn v Sunderland CC (2002) Laws LJ suggested that 'constitutional statutes', such as the ECA 1972, Magna Carta and the HRA, can be repealed only by express words or by words so specific that the inference of actual intention is irresistible. The Supreme Court in HS2 (2014) endorsed something similar, though the idea remains contested and it is unclear which statutes count.

questions.q: How does the UK constitution reflect a partial separation of powers?
markScheme: Montesquieu's theory explained briefly
Fusion of executive and legislature: ministers sit in Parliament, government controls Commons
Judicial independence strengthened by CRA 2005: Supreme Court, Lord Chancellor reform, JAC
Checks and balances: judicial review, privilege, Miller II
questions.modelAnswer: Montesquieu argued that liberty requires legislative, executive and judicial powers to be separate. The UK does not have a strict separation. Ministers must sit in Parliament, and a government with a Commons majority largely controls the legislative agenda, creating what Bagehot called the 'efficient secret' of fusion. The judiciary is more separate: the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 created the Supreme Court, removed the Lord Chancellor's judicial functions and established the Judicial Appointments Commission. Checks and balances operate through judicial review, parliamentary privilege and cases like Miller II (2019).

questions.q: Explain how CCSU (1985) changed judicial review of the prerogative.
markScheme: Before: courts would only determine existence and extent of prerogative
CCSU: prerogative powers reviewable in principle; focus on subject matter, not source
List of non-justiciable matters (treaties, defence, honours, dissolution, etc.)
Later cases (Bentley; Everett; Miller II) show expansion of reviewability
questions.modelAnswer: Traditionally courts would only decide whether a prerogative existed and its extent, not how it was exercised. In CCSU v Minister for the Civil Service (1985) the House of Lords held that the exercise of prerogative power is reviewable in principle; what matters is the subject matter rather than the source. Lord Roskill listed matters unsuitable for review, including treaties, defence, mercy, honours and dissolution. Later cases narrowed that list: ex p Bentley (1994) reviewed the mercy prerogative, ex p Everett (1989) passports, and Miller II (2019) prorogation.

questions.q: What is the Sewel Convention and what is its legal status?
markScheme: Westminster will not normally legislate on devolved matters without consent of devolved legislature
Recognised in Scotland Act 1998 s28(8) and Wales Act 2017
Miller I: non-justiciable political convention despite statutory recognition
questions.modelAnswer: The Sewel Convention states that the UK Parliament will not normally legislate with regard to devolved matters without the consent of the relevant devolved legislature. It was recognised in statute by the Scotland Act 2016, inserting s28(8) into the Scotland Act 1998, and by the Wales Act 2017. In Miller I (2017) the Supreme Court held that statutory recognition did not make the convention legally enforceable; it remains a political convention, as shown when Westminster passed Brexit legislation without devolved consent.

questions.q: Outline the requirements for a substantive legitimate expectation to be protected.
markScheme: Clear, unambiguous and unqualified representation or settled practice
Made by a person with actual or ostensible authority
Claimant within class to whom it was made; reliance relevant but not always required
Frustrating it must be justified: abuse of power / proportionality (Coughlan; Nadarajah)
Example: Coughlan 'home for life' promise
questions.modelAnswer: A substantive legitimate expectation arises from a clear, unambiguous and unqualified promise or established practice by a public body with authority to make it (R v IRC, ex p MFK Underwriting 1990). The claimant must be within the class to whom it was directed; detrimental reliance strengthens the claim but is not always essential. In ex p Coughlan (2001) a health authority's promise that a disabled resident would have a 'home for life' was enforced because breaking it was so unfair as to be an abuse of power. Later cases frame the question as whether frustrating the expectation is a proportionate response to a legitimate aim (Nadarajah 2005; Re Finucane 2019).

questions.q: Explain the limits of the interpretative obligation in s3 HRA 1998.
markScheme: Strong obligation to read compatibly 'so far as possible'
Ghaidan: may depart from ordinary meaning, read in words
Cannot go against the grain or a fundamental feature of the legislation
Re S: cannot make decisions requiring legislative deliberation
Where impossible, s4 declaration instead (Bellinger)
questions.modelAnswer: Section 3 requires legislation to be read compatibly with Convention rights so far as it is possible to do so. This is a strong duty: in Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza (2004) the House of Lords read words in, and the obligation does not depend on ambiguity. But it has limits. A court cannot adopt a meaning inconsistent with a fundamental feature of the legislation or go against its grain (Ghaidan). In Re S (2002) the court could not create a new system for supervising care orders, as that would amount to legislating. Where a compatible reading is impossible, as with the gender reassignment issue in Bellinger v Bellinger (2003), the court can only make a s4 declaration.

questions.q: Explain what happened to 'retained EU law' under the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023.
markScheme: EUWA 2018 converted EU law into retained EU law at end of transition period
2023 Act renamed it 'assimilated law' from 1 January 2024
Abolished the principle of supremacy of EU law and general principles for that law
Revoked listed instruments and eased departure from retained case law
questions.modelAnswer: The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 preserved EU-derived law in force at the end of the transition period as 'retained EU law', retaining some EU features such as supremacy over pre-exit domestic legislation. The Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 revoked a list of instruments at the end of 2023 and, from 1 January 2024, renamed the remainder 'assimilated law'. It abolished the principle of supremacy and general principles of EU law in relation to that law, and made it easier for courts to depart from retained EU case law.

questions.q: Compare Dicey's and Bingham's conceptions of the rule of law and explain which better describes modern UK case law.
markScheme: Dicey: no punishment without breach of law; equality before ordinary law; rights from common law
Bingham: eight principles including fundamental rights and international law
Formal versus substantive distinction (Raz)
Case law supporting substantive aspects: UNISON, Simms, Evans
Case law supporting formal aspects: Entick, M v Home Office
Reasoned conclusion that courts apply a mixed/thicker conception
questions.modelAnswer: Dicey's conception emphasised that no one is punished except for a breach of law established in ordinary courts, that officials are subject to the same law as citizens, and that rights flow from judicial decisions. It is broadly formal. Bingham set out eight principles, adding protection of fundamental human rights, fair adjudication and compliance with international obligations, making his conception substantive. Raz's formal view resists adding such values. Modern case law reflects both. Entick (1765) and M v Home Office (1994) are classic formal authorities, but UNISON (2017) on access to justice, Simms (2000) on the principle of legality and Evans (2015) show courts treating the rule of law as protecting substantive values. The modern approach is closer to Bingham's.

questions.q: State two conventions associated with ministerial responsibility.
markScheme: Collective responsibility: unanimity, confidentiality, confidence
Individual responsibility: accountable to Parliament for department; resign for personal misconduct
Ministerial Code records these; accountability vs responsibility distinction
questions.modelAnswer: Collective ministerial responsibility requires ministers to support government decisions publicly, to keep Cabinet discussions confidential, and requires the government to resign or seek dissolution if it loses the confidence of the Commons. Individual ministerial responsibility makes each minister answerable to Parliament for their department's conduct and requires resignation for serious personal misconduct or knowingly misleading Parliament. Both are recorded in the Ministerial Code, although in practice ministers rarely resign for departmental failures, distinguishing accountability from responsibility.

questions.q: In 2026 Parliament passes the Courts (Finality) Act, which states: 'No decision of the Immigration Appeals Board shall be questioned in any court on any ground whatsoever.' The Board rejects Amir's asylum claim after misinterpreting the definition of 'refugee'. Amir argues that no clause can stop the High Court correcting a clear error of law. Advise Amir on whether he can seek judicial review, and discuss what the case reveals about parliamentary sovereignty.
markScheme: Orthodox Diceyan sovereignty: courts must apply Acts
Principle of legality: strong presumption Parliament does not intend to oust review (Simms)
Anisminic: error of law makes decision a nullity, not a 'decision'
Privacy International: strict construction; obiter that courts determine limits of ouster
Contrast clear wording post-Privacy International and JRCA 2022 s2 model of explicit ouster
Jackson obiter on limits to sovereignty if Parliament abolished judicial review
Rule of law considerations (CRA 2005 s1; UNISON)
Likely outcome: courts may read down clause; uncertainty if wording explicitly covers nullities
Evaluation: tension between legal and political constitutionalism
questions.modelAnswer:
On the orthodox Diceyan view Parliament can make any law, and courts must give effect to a clear statutory provision. However, courts presume that Parliament does not intend to exclude access to the courts, applying the principle of legality: fundamental rights can be overridden only by express words or necessary implication (ex p Simms 2000).

In Anisminic v FCC (1969) a clause stating that a 'determination' could not be questioned did not protect a determination vitiated by error of law, because such an error made it a nullity, not a determination at all. The Board's misreading of 'refugee' is such an error. In R (Privacy International) v IPT (2019) the Supreme Court read down a clause protecting 'decisions (including decisions as to whether they have jurisdiction)', holding that it did not cover decisions involving errors of law. Lord Carnwath suggested, obiter, that it is ultimately for courts, not Parliament, to determine the limits of the rule of law, and that a clause ousting review of errors of law might not be given effect.

The Courts (Finality) Act uses broad language ('on any ground whatsoever'), but it does not expressly refer to nullities or errors of law. By contrast, the Cart ouster in the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 expressly addresses nullity, showing Parliament can oust review if it speaks very clearly. A court may therefore hold that this clause does not exclude review for errors of law, so Amir can bring a claim.

If Parliament had expressly excluded review of nullities, the courts would face the question raised obiter in Jackson v AG (2005): would they refuse to give effect to an Act abolishing judicial review? Lord Steyn and Baroness Hale suggested courts might, given the rule of law (Constitutional Reform Act 2005 s1; UNISON 2017).

The case reveals a tension between legislative supremacy and the courts' role as guardians of legality. In practice, the courts avoid direct confrontation by interpretation, preserving formal sovereignty while protecting judicial review. Amir is likely to be able to seek review.

questions.q: The Prime Minister advises the King to prorogue Parliament for eight weeks during a constitutional crisis over a contested trade treaty, stating that the government needs time to prepare a new legislative programme. The treaty is due to be ratified during the prorogation, and the government has not laid it before Parliament. A month later, the Prime Minister advises a dissolution. Advise a group of MPs on any legal challenges.
markScheme: Prorogation is a prerogative power exercised on PM's advice; justiciable (Miller II)
Miller II test: does prorogation frustrate Parliament's constitutional functions without reasonable justification
Length (8 weeks) and timing; need for justification beyond preparing programme
Remedy: declaration that prorogation is null
Treaty: CRAG 2010 Part 2 requires laying 21 sitting days before ratification; prorogation means no sitting days
Ratification without compliance would breach statute; exceptions under s22
Treaty cannot change domestic law without Act (Miller I; Case of Proclamations)
Dissolution: revived prerogative under DCPA 2022; s3 ouster clause
Interpretation of s3 in light of Privacy International; likely effective given explicit wording
Conventions on caretaker government/Lascelles Principles as political, not legal, limits
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Prorogation: proroguing Parliament is a prerogative act on the Prime Minister's advice. In Miller II/Cherry (2019) the Supreme Court held that the courts determine the limits of prerogative powers. A prorogation is unlawful if it has the effect of frustrating or preventing, without reasonable justification, Parliament's ability to carry out its constitutional functions as a legislature and as the body responsible for supervising the executive. An eight-week prorogation during a crisis is longer than the five weeks in Miller II. Preparing a legislative programme usually takes days, not weeks, and the court in Miller II found no adequate explanation for the length. If the government cannot justify it, the court is likely to declare the advice unlawful and the prorogation null.

The treaty: under Part 2 of the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010, a treaty must be laid before Parliament for 21 sitting days before ratification. During prorogation there are no sitting days, so the government cannot comply. Section 22 permits ratification without following this procedure only in exceptional cases, and the minister must then lay the treaty and explain why. Using prorogation to avoid scrutiny strengthens the argument that the prorogation was for an improper purpose. Moreover, ratification cannot change domestic law: if implementation requires legislation, an Act is needed (Case of Proclamations 1610; Miller I 2017).

Dissolution: the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 revived the prerogative to dissolve Parliament. Section 3 provides that a court may not question the exercise or purported exercise of that power, its limits or extent. Unlike the clauses in Anisminic and Privacy International, s3 is explicit and was drafted with those cases in mind. A court would probably accept it, though one might argue in light of Lord Carnwath's obiter in Privacy International that it cannot exclude review entirely. Constitutional conventions, such as the Lascelles Principles on the monarch refusing a dissolution, are political and not enforceable.

Conclusion: the MPs have a strong claim against the prorogation and a statutory argument over the treaty, but a challenge to dissolution is likely to fail.

questions.q: The Scottish Parliament passes the Scottish Energy Bill, which (a) bans new nuclear power stations in Scotland; (b) states that UK Acts on energy shall have no effect in Scotland without the Scottish Parliament's consent; and (c) sets up a Scottish nuclear safety regulator replacing the UK Office for Nuclear Regulation. Nuclear safety is a reserved matter. Advise on whether the Bill is within competence and what the UK Government can do.
markScheme: Reserved powers model; s29 limits; 'not law'
Test of 'relates to' reserved matters: purpose by reference to effect (s29(3); Martin v Most; UK Withdrawal from EU reference)
(a) planning/environment is devolved; ban via planning may be within competence if not relating to nuclear safety
(b) modifies s28(7) and Westminster sovereignty: outside competence (UNCRC reference)
(c) relates to reserved matter of nuclear safety: outside competence
Pre-assent referral to Supreme Court under s33
s35 order by Secretary of State
Westminster may legislate itself (s28(7)), Sewel political constraint
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The Scotland Act 1998 adopts a reserved powers model. Under s29 a provision is outside legislative competence, and 'not law', if it relates to reserved matters in Schedule 5, breaches Convention rights, modifies protected enactments in Schedule 4, among other limits. Whether a provision 'relates to' a reserved matter is determined by its purpose, having regard to its effect in all the circumstances (s29(3)); the connection must be more than loose or consequential (Martin v Most 2010; UK Withdrawal from the EU (Legal Continuity) (Scotland) Bill reference 2018).

(a) Banning new nuclear power stations: planning and the environment are generally devolved. The Scottish Government has used planning policy to oppose new nuclear stations. If the purpose of the ban is planning and environmental policy, it is probably within competence. If its purpose is to regulate nuclear safety or energy generation in a way relating to reserved matters, it may be outside competence. Careful drafting focusing on land use would help.

(b) Requiring Scottish consent for UK Acts: this purports to restrict Westminster's power to legislate for Scotland, which s28(7) preserves. In the UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Bill reference (2021) provisions affecting the effect of UK legislation in Scotland were outside competence because they modified s28(7), a protected enactment. Clause (b) is outside competence.

(c) Replacing the UK nuclear regulator: nuclear safety is reserved, so this plainly relates to a reserved matter and is outside competence.

UK Government options: the Advocate General may refer the Bill to the Supreme Court under s33 within four weeks of its passing, before royal assent. The Secretary of State may make a s35 order prohibiting submission for royal assent if provisions would make modifications of the law as it applies to reserved matters with reasonable grounds to believe they would adversely affect that law, as in the 2023 gender recognition order. Westminster could also legislate directly under s28(7), although the Sewel Convention imposes a political expectation of consent.

Conclusion: (b) and (c) are outside competence; (a) may survive depending on purpose.

questions.q: The Ministry of Culture runs a grant scheme for arts groups. Its published policy says applications will be judged on 'artistic merit and community benefit'. Splash Theatre's application is rejected without reasons. Splash learns the minister instructed officials to reject any group that had criticised government policy in the past year, and that the panel chair is married to the director of a rival theatre that received a grant. Splash's letter before claim was sent four months after the decision. Advise Splash.
markScheme: Amenability: public body exercising public function; reviewable
Procedural hurdles: permission, standing (sufficient interest), time limit: three months; delay and extension discretion
Illegality: improper purpose / irrelevant considerations (Padfield; Fewings)
Fettering discretion by blanket rule (British Oxygen)
Departure from published policy; legitimate expectation that policy will be applied (Mandalia; Lumba)
Procedural impropriety: bias: Porter v Magill test; chair's spouse interest
Reasons: no general duty but fairness may require (Doody; Oakley)
s31(2A) highly likely not substantially different test
Possible free expression (Article 10 HRA) argument
Remedies: quashing order, remittal
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Amenability and procedure: the ministry is a public body administering a public grant scheme, so its decision is reviewable. Splash has sufficient interest as a rejected applicant (s31(3) Senior Courts Act 1981). The main problem is time: claims must be brought promptly and in any event within three months (CPR 54.5). Splash is already outside that period. The court may extend time for good reason; Splash could argue it learnt of the minister's instruction only later, but it must act immediately.

Illegality: the minister instructed officials to reject groups that had criticised government policy. This is an improper purpose and an irrelevant consideration, not connected to the scheme's stated criteria of artistic merit and community benefit (Padfield 1968; ex p Fewings 1995). A blanket rule also fetters discretion (British Oxygen 1971). Departing from published criteria without good reason is itself unlawful, since applicants are entitled to have the stated policy applied (R (Lumba) v Home Secretary 2011; Mandalia v Home Secretary 2015) and may have a procedural legitimate expectation.

Bias: applying Porter v Magill (2001), the fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias where the panel chair's spouse directed a rival theatre competing for the same funds. The chair should have withdrawn. If the spouse's theatre benefited financially, there may be automatic disqualification (Dimes 1852), though that rule usually concerns the decision-maker's own interest.

Reasons: there is no general common law duty to give reasons, but fairness may require them where the decision is important and the applicant cannot otherwise challenge it (ex p Doody 1994). The lack of reasons supports an inference of irrationality.

Human rights: penalising groups for criticising government may engage Article 10 under the HRA.

Relief: the court is unlikely to refuse relief under s31(2A), since a properly applied scheme might well have produced a different outcome. A quashing order and reconsideration by an untainted panel would be appropriate.

Conclusion: strong grounds, but delay is a serious risk.

questions.q: The (fictional) Public Order (Protests) Act 2026, s5, allows police to 'impose any condition on a protest they consider necessary to prevent serious disruption'. Police ban a peaceful climate protest by Earth Now outside Parliament, citing possible traffic delays. Earth Now's leader, Lena, is arrested for attending. The Act also provides (s9) that a person convicted of an offence under it 'shall be barred from all public sector employment for life'. Advise Lena under the Human Rights Act 1998.
markScheme: Articles 10 and 11 engaged: peaceful assembly and expression (qualified rights)
Interference must be prescribed by law, pursue legitimate aim, and be necessary/proportionate
Police are public authority under s6; s6(2) defence if primary legislation requires act
s3: read 'necessary' and 'serious disruption' compatibly: proportionality requirement (DPP v Ziegler)
Proportionality: Bank Mellat four stages; blanket ban for traffic delay likely disproportionate
Remedy: damages under s8; challenge arrest
s9 lifetime ban: Article 8 (and Article 10) engagement; blanket nature
s3 reading impossible due to 'shall' and 'for life'; s4 declaration of incompatibility
Declaration does not invalidate (s4(6)); remedial order s10
Strasbourg case law under s2 (e.g. Kudrevičius on disruption)
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Lena can rely on Articles 10 (expression) and 11 (peaceful assembly), which protect peaceful protest even if it causes some disruption. Both are qualified: interference must be prescribed by law, pursue a legitimate aim such as preventing disorder or protecting others' rights, and be necessary in a democratic society, that is, proportionate.

The ban: the police are a public authority under HRA s6 and must act compatibly unless primary legislation requires them to act otherwise (s6(2)). Section 5 gives a discretion, not a duty, and under s3 the words 'necessary to prevent serious disruption' can readily be read as requiring a proportionate assessment. In DPP v Ziegler (2021) the Supreme Court held that a fact-specific proportionality assessment is required where obstruction offences are applied to protest. Applying Bank Mellat (2013): preventing disruption is a legitimate aim; a ban is rationally connected; but a less intrusive measure, such as conditions on location, timing or size, was available, and a total ban of a peaceful protest for mere traffic delays fails to strike a fair balance. Strasbourg case law, taken into account under s2, accepts that some disruption is inherent in assembly (Kudrevičius v Lithuania 2015). The ban is likely unlawful under s6, providing a defence to the arrest or a basis for challenging any conviction, with possible damages under s8.

The lifetime ban: s9 imposes an automatic lifetime employment bar. This interferes with Article 8 (private life, including professional life) and may deter protest in breach of Articles 10 and 11. A blanket, indiscriminate measure with no individual assessment is very difficult to justify as proportionate. Can it be read compatibly under s3? The words 'shall' and 'for life' express a fundamental feature of the provision; reading in a discretion would go against the grain (Ghaidan 2004; Re S 2002). A higher court could therefore make a declaration of incompatibility under s4. It would leave s9 valid (s4(6)) but permit a remedial order (s10).

Conclusion: Lena has a strong argument that the ban was unlawful, but s9 can be challenged only by a declaration of incompatibility.

questions.q: 'The UK's political constitution has served it well; codification would merely transfer power from Parliament to judges.' Discuss.
markScheme: Define political constitution (Griffith) and legal constitutionalism
Strengths of political constitution: flexibility, democratic accountability, evolution through convention
Weaknesses: executive dominance ('elective dictatorship', Hailsham), fragile conventions, reliance on 'good chaps'
Recent strains: Brexit, prorogation (Miller II), devolution tensions, Ministerial Code breaches
Courts already constrain: principle of legality, Miller I and II, HRA
Codification models: entrenched vs non-entrenched; judicial review of statutes
Transfer of power argument: whether entrenchment requires strike-down powers; alternatives (HRA-style declarations)
Democratic legitimacy of codification via constituent process
Balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Griffith's political constitution relies on Parliament, elections and political conventions rather than courts to restrain government. Its defenders point to flexibility, the capacity to evolve without formal amendment, and democratic accountability: elected representatives, not unelected judges, settle contested questions of rights and policy.

There are strong reasons to think it has served the UK reasonably well. Major reforms, such as devolution, the HRA and the Constitutional Reform Act 2005, were introduced through ordinary legislation without crisis. Conventions adapt to new circumstances, such as the practice of seeking Commons approval for military action.

Yet its weaknesses have become more visible. Lord Hailsham warned of an 'elective dictatorship': a government with a secure majority controls Parliament. The constitution depends on politicians observing conventions in good faith, which Hennessy described as the 'good chaps' theory. The Brexit period exposed these strains: the 2019 prorogation required intervention in Miller II, the Sewel Convention was overridden, and disputes over the Ministerial Code showed the limits of self-regulation.

The courts have already developed significant constraints without codification: the principle of legality (Simms 2000), control of the prerogative (Miller I and II), and interpretation under the HRA. So the claim that codification would introduce judicial power ignores that judges already play a substantial role.

Whether codification transfers power depends on design. An entrenched constitution with judicial strike-down powers would shift power to judges significantly. But a codified document could be non-entrenched, or could rely on HRA-style declarations of incompatibility that leave the final word with Parliament. A codified constitution could also strengthen Parliament, for example by setting out its control over prorogation, treaty-making and war powers.

The democratic objection is also weaker if a constitution were adopted through a deliberative process with popular endorsement, giving it greater legitimacy than many current arrangements.

In conclusion, the political constitution has proved adaptable, but it is fragile when conventions are not respected. Codification need not transfer power wholesale to judges; the real choice is about what balance between political and legal accountability the UK wants.

questions.q: 'After Brexit, the orthodox Diceyan account of parliamentary sovereignty is once again an accurate description of UK constitutional law.' Discuss.
markScheme: Dicey's account: positive and negative limbs; no binding successors
EU membership challenge: Factortame disapplication; Thoburn explanation
Brexit: ECA repealed; EUWA s5; REUL Act 2023 abolished supremacy
Remaining Factortame-like effect: EUWA s7A and Windsor Framework; Allister
HRA: preserves sovereignty formally (s3/s4) but strong interpretive pressure
Common law constitutionalism: Jackson obiter, Privacy International, principle of legality
Manner and form/new view; Parliament Acts
